## TL;DR

Check gates now hold a task-scoped lock across handoff validation, managed engineer self-checks, direct CLI checks in a task worktree, and close-out validation. RepoOS queues task bookkeeping commits while a gate is active and replays each commit in order after the last holder exits. Drift detection checks every newly reachable commit and reports source-affecting subjects and paths; bookkeeping-only changes are ignored. Review 8's accepted limitation remains: a filesystem write by an engineer already running cannot be fenced. Such committed source edits are detected after the check and invalidate its result.

## Work and rationale

The self-check lock now starts before remote validation. In managed runs, the remote helper may own a nested holder, but the outer holder remains until the local plan ends, preventing the remote-to-local gap from releasing protection. A normal `repoos check` in a task worktree discovers its task ID from the worktree branch and takes the same lock. The work-in-progress checkpoint is still written before the lock starts so it is not blocked by its own gate. Lock failure is surfaced rather than allowing an unprotected check to continue. Error and local-slot failure paths release the holder; normal local plan completion also releases it in `finally`. Handoff and close-out already acquire their task locks for the complete validation window and release through their own `finally` paths.

The bookkeeping queue stores explicit write and delete snapshots at enqueue time, so an empty file and a removed file remain distinct operations. Queue and holder updates share a cross-process state mutex. A directory left behind without its PID is reclaimed only after its initialization grace period. Flush persists a pending entry before changing files, then records the intermediate expected snapshot after every successful commit. If a commit fails, its queue entry remains. If a process stops between a Git commit and the queue update, recovery uses the pending parent, subject, and snapshots to recognize that commit and advance exactly once. Release and stale-lock recovery flush before clearing the task lock, so another check cannot enter the gap.

Drift inspection enumerates all commits in the new `base..HEAD` range, including commits introduced through side branches. For a merge commit it compares the tree to the first parent, the checked branch. This captures source commits that are later reverted while avoiding false positives for source already present at check start but absent from a side branch's second parent. A failed history or path query fails closed; refusals include each available commit subject and changed source paths.

Direct filesystem writes by an already-running engineer are an accepted limitation. RepoOS does not claim to intercept arbitrary writes. The managed start guard prevents a new engineer session from starting under the lock, RepoOS-controlled source commits are refused, and post-check drift detection rejects a committed source change with its subject and paths. This limitation and behavior are documented in `docs/check-run-history.md`, `docs/agent-workflow-rules.md`, and `user-docs/check.md`.

## Approaches tried

Review 8 clarified that the recurring source-write finding was an accepted limitation, so I removed any expectation of filesystem fencing and documented after-the-fact detection. For queue recovery, an in-memory cursor was insufficient because a crash could happen after a commit reached Git but before the cursor was persisted. I used an on-disk pending journal containing the pre-commit HEAD, message, prior snapshots, and intended snapshots; recovery reconciles that journal against Git before advancing the durable queue. Replay now records its progress after each committed entry, preserving the exact order of repeated writes.

The first replay implementation failed focused tests because it called the asynchronous `runGit` API as if it returned a result synchronously. I isolated the queue flush path, confirmed it stopped before processing the pending entry, and switched the synchronous recovery reads to `gitCapture`. The focused queue tests then passed, including failed-commit retry, repeated writes, deletions, and stale-lock recovery.

## Challenges and blockers

The remote check hung on the first runner (`thinkpad`). RepoOS killed that validation container and retried on `bee`; the retry acquired a slot and completed successfully. It uploaded and verified the task branch, rebuilt, and passed the scoped test selection, UI smoke, and rendered contrast audit. The local phase then passed staleness rebuild, format, lint, build, source guards, smoke, and user docs build. No unresolved implementation blocker remains.

## Key learnings

The queue's durable state must describe both the intended file contents and where replay stopped; a single final snapshot cannot safely represent several queued commits touching the same file. A mutex needs recovery for the directory-creation-before-PID crash window, and it must be held across the complete read-modify-write operation. Git traversal also needs two distinct rules: inspect every commit reachable after the starting HEAD, but measure each merge's own delta against its first parent. Finally, source-write protection has a clear boundary: RepoOS can refuse its own writes and new managed sessions, while direct filesystem writes from an existing process are handled by post-check drift detection.
